question_blueprint.learning_objective: Explain how molecular size and polarizability influence boiling point through London dispersion forces.
question_blueprint.target_misconception: Nonpolar molecules are believed to have negligible or no intermolecular forces, so they are expected to always have low boiling points compared with polar molecules.
question_blueprint.correct_answer_concept: All molecules experience London dispersion forces, and for sufficiently large or highly polarizable nonpolar molecules these forces can outweigh dipole-dipole attractions in smaller polar molecules, leading to higher boiling points.
question_blueprint.expected_reasoning: Students must compare a larger nonpolar molecule with a smaller polar molecule, recognize that dispersion strength increases with electron cloud size/polarizability and surface contact, and conclude that boiling point depends on overall IMF strength, not simply on whether a molecule is polar.
question_blueprint.question_style_notes: Use a ranking or comparison among molecules such as halogens or hydrocarbons versus a small polar molecule. Ensure the key depends on dispersion increasing with size. Include a distractor stating that nonpolar substances have no IMFs and another stating that any polar molecule must boil higher than any nonpolar molecule.

last_candidate.question: Butane (C4H10) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) have different boiling points. Which substance is expected to have the higher boiling point, and why?

options.A: HCl, because its permanent dipole means dipole-dipole attractions are stronger than dispersion forces in all cases.
options.B: C4H10, because its larger, more polarizable electron cloud produces stronger overall London dispersion forces.
options.C: HCl, because C4H10 is nonpolar and therefore has only negligible intermolecular attractions.
options.D: C4H10, because nonpolar molecules of similar size usually boil at higher temperatures than polar molecules.

last_candidate.explanation: All molecules, including nonpolar ones, experience London dispersion forces. Butane is nonpolar, but it is larger and more polarizable than HCl, so its dispersion forces are stronger overall than the intermolecular attractions between HCl molecules. Therefore, butane has the higher boiling point; this is consistent with the actual boiling points, with butane boiling above HCl.
